```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                    fig.height = 3.5)
library(lifeconformal)
```

The workflow has two estimation steps. `life_train()` fits a score and nuisance
models on training subjects. `life_calibrate()` uses independent subjects to
calibrate that fixed score. `predict()` then produces regions for new baseline
covariates. This version does not split samples automatically or use cross-fitting.

## Prepare observed histories

Use one row per observed state entry or end of follow-up. Every row carries a
subject identifier, time since the common prediction origin, an event status,
and any baseline covariates. Status zero always denotes censoring or the end of
observation. Other status values identify destination states by default.

This three-subject table illustrates a process with state zero (event-free),
state one (relapse), and absorbing state two (death):

```{r input-table}
toy <- data.frame(
  id = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 3),
  time = c(1, 3, 5, 2, 4),
  status = c(1, 2, 0, 1, 0),
  age = c(60, 60, 55, 70, 70)
)
knitr::kable(toy)
```

Subject 1 enters state one at time one and state two at time three. Subject 2
is censored at time five without a transition. Subject 3 enters state one at
time two and is censored at time four. All begin in state zero; no artificial
event at zero is required. Covariates stay constant within a subject, and records
must already be chronologically ordered. The package rejects ambiguous tied
transitions, missing required values, and inconsistent histories.

Input checks run before fitting and report the affected field and, when
available, the subject and original input row. For example:

```{r invalid-time}
invalid <- toy
invalid$time[2] <- NA_real_
tryCatch(
  life_train(LifeHist(time, status) ~ age, data = invalid,
             absorbing = 2, targets = list(relapse_free = 0), tau = 5),
  error = conditionMessage
)
```

Correct the source record and rerun the call. Records are neither discarded nor
reordered automatically. These requirements also apply to calibration histories:

| Field or record | Required format |
| --- | --- |
| Identifiers | One nonmissing, nonempty identifier per row; repeated values identify the same subject |
| Times | Finite, nonnegative elapsed times in chronological order within subject; actual transitions occur after time zero |
| Status | Zero ends observation; other codes must map to the destination state |
| Final record | A censoring record or entry into a declared absorbing state; no subsequent records |
| Baseline covariates | Observed values that remain constant within subject |
| New covariates | Training-compatible types, factor levels, and valid formula-transformation domains |

Two transitions at the same time are ambiguous. A transition followed by a
censoring record at that same time is allowed. Explicit intervals additionally
require contiguous times and a `from` state matching the preceding destination.
Errors describe the relevant rule rather than inferring an unobserved transition.

The table explains the format; it is too small to illustrate model fitting well.
For a runnable analysis, generate independent synthetic subjects with one possible
transition, from state zero to terminal state two:

```{r synthetic-data}
histories <- life_example_data(n = 120, seed = 1)
head(histories)
```

These artificial data include a mild age association, independent censoring
conditional on age, and administrative follow-up ending at time eight. Times use
arbitrary units. They make no clinical or statistical performance claim. The
data generator uses simulation; the default Markov prediction calculations below
are deterministic.

Keep all records for a subject in one sample. The generated subjects are
independent and identically generated, so using the first 80 for training is a
simple reproducible split. For observational data, choose a split appropriate to
the study design before fitting or evaluating models.

```{r split-subjects}
training_ids <- unique(histories$id)[seq_len(80)]
training <- histories[histories$id %in% training_ids, , drop = FALSE]
calibration <- histories[!histories$id %in% training_ids, , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(length(intersect(training$id, calibration$id)) == 0)
```

## Train the score and working models

Predict occupation time in state zero through time five. With a single
transition to death, this is survival time restricted to the horizon.

```{r train}
fit <- life_train(
  LifeHist(time, status) ~ age,
  data = training,
  absorbing = 2,
  targets = list(alive = 0),
  tau = 5
)
fit
```

The formula selects the age predictor; other data columns do not enter the
model automatically. The defaults use identifier column `id`, initial state
zero, Cox censoring regression, and transition-specific Markov-Cox outcome
intensities. The outcome fit supplies target means and scales for the score and
is reused for augmentation. The target, horizon, and absorbing states are explicit.

The fitted object contains reusable functions and all fitted preprocessing.
Predicting from the training fit returns the score's moments, before calibration:

```{r trained-moments}
new_patients <- data.frame(id = c("new-1", "new-2"), age = c(50, 70))
moments <- predict(fit, newdata = new_patients)
moments$mean
moments$scale
```

## Calibrate independently, then predict

Augmented inverse-probability weighting is the default. The same trained object
also supports the IPW estimator:

```{r calibrate}
cal_aipw <- life_calibrate(fit, data = calibration, alpha = 0.10)
cal_ipw <- life_calibrate(fit, data = calibration, alpha = 0.10,
                         method = "ipw")
cal_aipw
cal_ipw
```

IPW uses observed coverage determinations and censoring weights. Augmentation
also uses conditional coverage given partial histories. The IPW branch skips
those conditional-coverage predictions and augmentation sums. Neither call
refits the score or nuisance models.

```{r calibrated-predictions}
regions <- predict(cal_aipw, newdata = new_patients)
regions$bounds
predict(cal_ipw, newdata = new_patients)$bounds
```

Bounds use the time units of the data and are intersected with the target's
structural support. Here that support is `[0, 5]`. A returned full-support region
is an explicit possible result, including when a small sample cannot reach the
requested rank-adjusted cutoff or the estimated curve does not cross it.

The requested 90% level is nominal. Its interpretation requires the method's
sampling, censoring, positivity, and nuisance-estimation assumptions. IPW
requires a consistent estimate of the censoring distribution. Augmented
calibration attains at least nominal coverage asymptotically if either the
censoring model or the conditional coverage model is correct, under the
corresponding convergence conditions.

Inspect the raw coverage curve and numerical diagnostics:

```{r diagnostics}
cal_aipw$full_support
cal_aipw$reason
cal_aipw$diagnostics$numerical
cal_ipw$diagnostics$numerical
```

```{r coverage-curve}
plot(cal_aipw)
```

The dashed line is the actual rank-adjusted cutoff. The package takes the first
crossing on the supplied threshold grid. Raw estimated coverage can be nonmonotone;
signed augmented contributions are retained. The method does not smooth or clip
the curve to make it look like a distribution function.

Save the calibrated object to retain its frozen models, preprocessing, target
definitions, and threshold:

```{r save-and-restore}
saved <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(cal_aipw, saved)
restored <- readRDS(saved)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(predict(restored, new_patients)$bounds,
                           regions$bounds)))
unlink(saved)
```

## Other data interfaces and states

The vector interface has the same computation and accepts a named covariate
matrix or data frame:

```{r vector-interface}
fit_vectors <- life_train(
  x = training["age"], id = training$id,
  time = training$time, status = training$status,
  absorbing = 2, targets = list(alive = 0), tau = 5
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(predict(fit_vectors, new_patients)$mean,
                           moments$mean)))
```

Use the same representation for its calibration sample:

```{r vector-calibration}
cal_vectors <- life_calibrate(
  fit_vectors,
  x = calibration["age"], id = calibration$id,
  time = calibration$time, status = calibration$status,
  method = "ipw"
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(predict(cal_vectors, new_patients)$bounds,
                           predict(cal_ipw, new_patients)$bounds)))
```

Explicit transition intervals are also supported. For the single-transition
synthetic example, the equivalent input is:

```{r explicit-intervals}
interval_training <- transform(
  training, start = 0, stop = time, from = 0,
  to = ifelse(status == 2, 2, NA_real_), event = status == 2
)
fit_intervals <- life_train(
  LifeHist(start = start, stop = stop, from = from, to = to, event = event) ~ age,
  data = interval_training,
  absorbing = 2, targets = list(alive = 0), tau = 5
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(predict(fit_intervals, new_patients,
                                   initial_state = 0)$mean,
                           moments$mean)))
```

For event-status data, `initial_state = 0` is the default. Set a common different
label with `initial_state = "home"`, or use a baseline column, such as
`initial_state = ~ baseline_state`, when subjects start in different states.
That column must be constant within subject and supplied for new patients.
For explicit intervals, an omitted initial state is inferred from the first
`from` value; then provide `initial_state` when predicting for new subjects, as
above, or specify a common initial state explicitly during training.
Absorbing states are always declared; use `absorbing = c(3, 4)` for
two terminal states or `absorbing = integer(0)` for none. States without observed
exits are not automatically absorbing.

A return to state zero needs a nonzero event code because status zero remains
reserved for censoring. For example:

```{r return-to-zero}
return_example <- data.frame(
  id = c(1, 1, 1), time = c(2, 4, 7), status = c(1, 3, 0),
  age = c(60, 60, 60)
)
status_map <- c("1" = 1, "2" = 2, "3" = 0)
return_example
```

This patient enters state one at time two, returns to state zero at time four,
and is censored at time seven. Supply this `status_map` in `life_train()` when
analyzing a suitably sized dataset with that encoding. A terminal entry completes
the path, so it does not require a final censoring row. A subject initially in an
absorbing state is already complete at the origin.

For the three-state relapse/death example, a joint target specification could be
`targets = list(event_free = 0, alive = c(0, 1))`. A common maximum standardized
score then calibrates the target vector jointly. Returned coordinate bounds are
conservative envelopes of that joint region’s coordinate projections; its
overlap and support constraints are retained.

The fitted transition graph uses transitions observed in training. Structural
support is separate: an absent empirical transition does not prove that it is
impossible. Only supply `allowed_transitions` when the restriction is substantively
known, for example a from/to table describing an established progressive process.

## Choose working models and computation

Censoring and outcome choices are independent:

| Component | Default | Alternatives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Censoring | `"cox"` | `"survival_forest"` |
| Outcome | `"markov_cox"` | `"transition_forest"`, `"transition_neural"` |

Specify a different censoring predictor formula with `censor_formula`, and pass
backend controls in `censor_options` and `outcome_options`. For example, this keeps
the deterministic Markov outcome model and selects a censoring forest:

```{r censor-forest, eval=FALSE}
fit_with_forest_censor <- life_train(
  LifeHist(time, status) ~ age, data = training,
  absorbing = 2, targets = list(alive = 0), tau = 5,
  censor_model = "survival_forest",
  censor_options = list(num_trees = 200L, min_node_size = 10L),
  seed = 11
)
```

This option requires `ranger`. Outcome intensity forests instead use `rpart`
exposure/count trees with whole-subject bootstrap sampling. The neural option
uses a tanh/softplus transition-intensity network fitted by `stats::optim()`.
Both flexible outcome families can use duration in state and previous transitions.
They use reproducible continuation draws for target prediction and augmentation;
the Markov-Cox branch uses deterministic recursions throughout.

These optional examples are shown without executing the additional model fits
when building the introduction:

```{r flexible-outcomes, eval=FALSE}
fit_tree <- life_train(
  LifeHist(time, status) ~ age, data = training,
  absorbing = 2, targets = list(alive = 0), tau = 5,
  outcome_model = "transition_forest",
  outcome_options = list(num_trees = 100L, step_size = 0.1),
  control = list(draws = 1000L), seed = 12
)

fit_neural <- life_train(
  LifeHist(time, status) ~ age, data = training,
  absorbing = 2, targets = list(alive = 0), tau = 5,
  outcome_model = "transition_neural",
  outcome_options = list(hidden = 4L, decay = 0.01,
                         maxit = 1000L, step_size = 0.1),
  control = list(draws = 1000L), seed = 13
)
```

The model and numeric controls are recorded in the fitted object. For Cox models,
`ties = "breslow"` is the default and `"efron"` is available. The default scale
floor is `0.01 * tau`; fitted censoring survival is floored at `1e-8`. A survival
floor truncates inverse weights and changes the estimator, so inspect positivity
and sensitivity instead of interpreting the floor as evidence of adequate follow-up.

Direct working-probability prediction uses `grid_size = 128L`,
`max_nodes = 100000L`, and `probability_tolerance = 0.01` by default. Calibration
uses `calibration_accuracy = "auto"`: with Markov augmentation it starts at
grid16, unless a grid was explicitly supplied, and refines until signed numerical
bounds establish the first crossing over the fixed threshold grid. Other
probabilities may remain less precise; inspect `threshold_stable` and
`probability_tolerance_met` separately. To enforce precision for every conditional
probability, supply `control = list(calibration_accuracy = "probability")`.
Numerical brackets describe discretization uncertainty in the fitted
distribution, excluding floating-point rounding. They are separate from
statistical coverage guarantees and are not coverage confidence intervals. An unresolved threshold or exhausted resource
budget gives an informative error. Markov calculations remain deterministic.

For flexible outcomes, decrease `outcome_options$step_size` to refine the time
approximation and increase `control$draws` to examine Monte Carlo precision.
Refit and recalibrate when changing the trained score's numerical specification.
Model tuning belongs to training data. Do not tune the score using the independent
calibration outcomes and then describe it as frozen.

## Reproducing an analysis

For reproducible analyses, retain the script, fitted object, chosen settings,
and `sessionInfo()`. Training and calibration identifiers should identify subjects
consistently across samples; separate numbering alone must not disguise reuse of
the same subjects.
